extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students preparing for the Putnam Competition
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and concrete procedures for studying for and taking the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition, including subject-matter coverage, exam-day tactics, and how to write solutions for grading. Targeted at undergraduates preparing to compete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter of the exam
rubrics_metrics.description: The Putnam exam is based mainly on the beginning subjects of an undergraduate mathematics major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample topics listed: polynomials (factoring, Fundamental Theorem of Algebra), set theory (countability, one-to-one correspondences), combinatorics (pigeonhole, graphs, coloring), recurrence (linear recurrences, induction), linear algebra (independence, bases, determinants), number theory (congruences, FLT, quadratic reciprocity, approximations), binomials, abstract algebra (rings, isomorphisms), finite fields, group theory (Lagrange, characters), geometry (analytic, conic sections, inequalities, special triangle points), inequalities (Cauchy-Schwarz, AM-GM), limits/continuity (squeeze theorem), functional equations, extremal problems, differential and integral calculus techniques, probability, series, vector calculus (Stokes/Green), differential equations. Use this list to guide study and problem classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write-up and exposition quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Solutions must include all exposition necessary to justify the solution and be written clearly in grammatically correct full sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may use standard abbreviations like ⇔ for 'if and only if', but each key point must be presented clearly and in an orderly fashion. The write-up is extremely important; missing key points typically yields little credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the answer at the start
rubrics_metrics.description: Always state the answer at the beginning of your write-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample solution begins with 'The maximum value is 18.' Stating the answer up front helps graders and is explicitly recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring scale and partial credit expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each problem is graded on a 10-point scale; partial credit is difficult to obtain on the Putnam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because partial credit is hard to get, presentation of key logical steps is crucial. Nonetheless, if you state answers clearly you may gain some credit for a correct answer even without a full correct proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam format and eligibility rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure and administrative rules of the exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exam consists of two three-hour sessions with six problems each. It is open to undergraduates; a student may take it at most four times. Administrative: be sure all solution folders and extra pages turned in have an ID sticker.

rubrics_metrics.name: General preparation tenets
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad study philosophy for improving Putnam performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more mathematics you know, the better you'll do. Most Putnam problems are based on classic techniques from mainstream mathematics. Emphasize the theorems used and categorize problems by branch to bring relevant techniques to mind. Olympiad-style training and working many problems improves skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial exam reading routine
rubrics_metrics.description: How to begin each session on exam day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by reading all six problems completely through once without writing anything. Then read them again and make notes (category, underline data, estimate difficulty, devise order of attack).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem classification and note-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading problems, note the branch of math, underline important data, and estimate difficulty to order work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit checklist when re-reading: (a) what category (calculus, linear algebra, number theory), (b) underline the data, (c) estimate difficulty and devise order. A-1 and B-1 are usually easiest but may not be for a given year or student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time allocation and 'move-on' rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit time spent on any single problem and move on if progress stalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate at most 30 minutes to any given problem; if you haven't solved it in that time, move on to the next. In the final 15 minutes of the session, transfer whatever partial work you have to the solution folders to attempt to gain partial credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scratch-work-first practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Work on scratch paper first; do not write in solution folders until you have a coherent solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start work on the chosen problem on scratch paper only. If you solve it, take time to carefully transfer your work to the solution folder—presentation matters for grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final transfer and clarity of answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Before submission, transfer solutions/partial work clearly and ensure answers are stated plainly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the last 15 minutes, transfer partial work to the folders. State answers clearly; clear answers can sometimes earn credit even if proofs are incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the problem and underline key data
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin work on a problem by writing the problem verbatim and marking important data and phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes it helps to copy the problem word-for-word on scratch paper and underline all important data and phrases to avoid misreading and to focus on constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: List relevant facts and theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down all facts and theorems you can think of that might apply to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making an explicit list of relevant results helps identify applicable techniques and gives leads for solution paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break problems into subproblems and simplify
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to decompose the problem into easier subproblems and consider reduced versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the problem into manageable parts; reduce number of variables or dimensions to solve an easier version which may suggest the full solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagrams and notation carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw pictures and introduce clear notation for quantities; use subscripts when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw and redraw pictures until they match all data. Introduce notation for all quantities, be careful to use distinct symbols for distinct quantities, and be comfortable with subscripts and double-subscripts for sets of variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: State relations and frequently re-read the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state all relations among quantities and keep rereading the problem to avoid misunderstandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List all possible relations between quantities given in the problem, and frequently reread the problem to ensure no hypothesis or constraint is overlooked. Check that you use all hypotheses before finishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scratch-paper management and legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage scratch work for efficiency and legibility; avoid erasing and leave space for corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To save time, never erase on scratch paper. Write large and leave plenty of space for corrections. For long formulas, orient paper with the long side horizontal. If much crossing out is needed, start a fresh sheet and copy over the good parts.
